                    ### Question
                    A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of fever, productive cough, and shortness of breath. Since birth, he has had multiple respiratory infections requiring treatment with antibiotics. His immunizations are up-to-date. He is in the 10th percentile for height and weight. His temperature is 38°C (100.3°F). Examination detects diffuse bilateral wheezing and cervical lymphadenopathy. Flow cytometric analysis of a serum sample from the patient fails to fluoresce after incubation with dihydrorhodamine. This patient is at greatest risk of infection with which of the following organisms?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Enterococcus faecium
opb. Serratia marcescens
opc. Streptococcus pneumoniae
opd. Clostridioides difficile
ope. Streptococcus pyogenes

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 2-year-old boy presents with recurrent respiratory infections, fever, productive cough, and wheezing, indicating a possible underlying immunodeficiency. The flow cytometric analysis shows failure to fluoresce after incubation with dihydrorhodamine, suggesting a defect in the oxidative burst, consistent with chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). Patients with CGD are particularly susceptible to catalase-positive organisms due to their impaired ability to kill these pathogens. Among the options provided, Serratia marcescens is a catalase-positive organism and is known to cause infections in patients with CGD. Therefore, the patient is at greatest risk of infection with Serratia marcescens.
